messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Keanu had always taken pride in his precision. For fifty years as an editor, his life was built on the careful arrangement of words, on spotting the flaw in a line of reasoning, on the quiet authority of a red pen. That world of order shattered seven months ago. The man he had loved, Alex, had a temper that could curdle the air in their apartment. It often began with criticism—a misplaced book, a meal cooked imperfectly—that would escalate into a tirade, and then, finally, into violence. The last time, Alex’s critique of a political opinion Keanu had shared ended with Keanu on the floor, the sharp pain in his ribs a counterpoint to the cold shock of betrayal. He left the next day and never returned, but the event did not stay in the past.

The trauma doesn't live in his mind as a story. Instead, he describes it as a series of still photographs, stark and silent: Alex’s face tightening with rage, a fist blurring towards him, the pattern of the rug inches from his eyes. When these images surface, Keanu feels an intense, volcanic rage, but it is a rage without an object, hot and useless. He often feels as if he’s watching a film about a stranger; he insists the memory “feels like it belongs to someone else,” a detached horror that is somehow more terrifying than feeling it as his own. He has come to believe this is his fault, that the abuse happened “because of the sort of person I am”—too quiet, too yielding, too easy a target. This conviction of his own flawed character haunts the edges of every memory, making the snapshots feel not just tragic, but deserved.

This sense of personal responsibility now dictates his life. At work, any form of correction has become a potent threat. Last week, a junior editor gently pointed out a continuity error he had missed in a manuscript. The quiet, professional criticism was all it took. Instantly, a snapshot of Alex’s face, contorted in disgust, flashed in Keanu’s mind. The memory ignited a surge of panic, and to escape it, he abruptly stood up, mumbled an excuse about needing coffee, and fled to the breakroom. He busied himself with the meticulous task of wiping down the counters, focusing on the repetitive motion until the image receded. This has become his primary method for survival: when a trigger appears—a violent scene on the news, a glimpse of a man who looks like Alex from behind—he immediately distracts himself, a frantic search for any neutral task to occupy his mind.

This constant campaign of avoidance has had profound consequences. By relentlessly distracting himself and refusing to allow any strong emotion to take hold, Keanu has starved his own emotional life. The strategy has reinforced his deepest fear: that he “will never be able to feel normal emotions again.” The snapshots of the trauma remain unprocessed, locked away like dangerous artifacts, their power growing in the dark. This emotional numbing, in turn, makes him feel less than human, as though he has become an object that simply reacts to stimuli. His avoidance has also made him exquisitely sensitive to triggers; because he actively avoids anything that might remind him of Alex, an unexpected encounter feels catastrophic, proving his world is still unsafe. The memory itself has become its own trigger; a quiet evening can be ruined by a fleeting image of the assault, which then sends him into a state of high alert, scanning for the next threat.

He has not seen Alex since he left, but the fear of it is a wall around his life. He avoids their old neighbourhood, their favourite restaurants, and any place that might hold a memory. This avoidance, this constant, exhausting vigilance, has cemented his belief that he is fundamentally broken. The logic feels simple and brutal to him: a whole person would be able to move on, but he cannot, so he must be a damaged thing. He sought therapy after the incident at work. His manager had noticed his increasingly erratic behaviour and expressed concern. For Keanu, it was the final humiliation. He came to his first session not with hope, but with a quiet resignation, asking if it was possible to fix someone who felt more like a collection of broken pieces than a man.
